presentingComplaint: Progressive breathlessness and difficulty clearing secretions over 3 days in a woman with known myasthenia gravis
history: Known acetylcholine-receptor-antibody-positive generalised myasthenia gravis for 4 years, maintained on pyridostigmine and low-dose prednisolone. Over the past week she developed a coryzal upper-respiratory illness, and in the last 72 hours has noted worsening fatigable ptosis, diplopia, nasal regurgitation of fluids, weak cough and progressive breathlessness that is worse when lying flat. Steroid dose was recently tapered by her GP. No chest pain. She reports difficulty finishing sentences today. Precipitant appears to be intercurrent viral infection plus steroid taper.
examination: Alert and oriented but visibly anxious and using accessory muscles of respiration; unable to complete a sentence in one breath. Bilateral fatigable ptosis and complex ophthalmoplegia, weak neck flexion, nasal dysarthria and a poor 'wet' cough with pooling of oral secretions. Fatigable proximal limb weakness. Single-breath count 12. Pertinent negatives: no fever, no meningism, pupils normal and reactive (not pinpoint), no fasciculations, no excess sweating/salivation to suggest cholinergic crisis, reflexes present, sensation intact.

labs.ABG: pH 7.31, PaCO2 6.9 kPa (52 mmHg), PaO2 9.0 kPa on air — early hypercapnic respiratory failure
labs.FVC: 0.9 L (approx 15 mL/kg) and falling on serial measurement

imaging: Chest radiograph: low lung volumes, basal atelectasis, no consolidation. CT thorax previously showed no thymoma.
microbiology: n/a — respiratory viral swab sent for precipitant identification; no evidence of bacterial infection
finalDiagnosis: Myasthenic crisis (neuromuscular respiratory failure) precipitated by intercurrent viral infection and steroid taper
citations: Harrison 22e — Myasthenia Gravis and Other Diseases of the Neuromuscular Junction
AAN/Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America (MGFA) International Consensus Guidance for Management of Myasthenia Gravis 2021
stewardship: not applicable — non-infective (neuromuscular respiratory failure). Antibiotics only if a bacterial precipitant is proven; avoid aminoglycosides, macrolides and fluoroquinolones which worsen neuromuscular transmission.
contraindications: Caution with beta-blockers and high-dose corticosteroid initiation (may transiently worsen weakness); IVIG relatively contraindicated in IgA deficiency / high thrombotic risk
edgeCases: Cholinergic crisis from anticholinesterase overuse mimics myasthenic crisis but shows miosis, hypersalivation, fasciculations, cramps and bradycardia — misclassification is dangerous
Do not be reassured by 'normal' SpO2 and PaO2: neuromuscular failure causes CO2 retention and abrupt collapse; trend FVC/NIF, not oximetry
Steroid initiation can transiently worsen weakness in the first 1-2 weeks
expectedMaiK: This is impending neuromuscular respiratory failure from a myasthenic crisis; act on falling serial FVC/NIF and rising PaCO2 rather than SpO2, arrange ICU/HDU with elective airway support, and start IVIG or plasma exchange while treating the precipitant. Avoid drugs that impair neuromuscular transmission.
expectedNextQuestions: Is this a myasthenic or cholinergic crisis (pupils, secretions, fasciculations, recent pyridostigmine dosing)?
What are the serial FVC and negative inspiratory force trends?
What precipitated it — infection, drug change, surgery, or steroid taper?
expectedInvestigations: Serial bedside spirometry (FVC) and negative inspiratory force
Screen for precipitant (viral swab / infection screen), and repeat acetylcholine-receptor antibody status if diagnosis uncertain

investigations: Serial forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force

regressionAssertions: must not classify as CAP/pneumonia given afebrile, clear chest and normal WCC/CRP
must flag neuromuscular respiratory failure requiring FVC/NIF monitoring, not SpO2 reassurance
